hook: David Rumelhart earned a bachelors degree in psychology and mathematics from the University of South Dakota before completing a PhD in mathematical psychology at Stanford University in 1967. He then joined the faculty at the University of California, San Diego, where he helped build the Parallel Distributed Processing research group that modeled cognition as patterns of activity distributed across networks of simple units. With Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, he co-authored the 1986 Nature paper Learning Representations by Back Propagating Errors, which showed how multilayer neural networks could be trained efficiently and became one of the founding texts of modern deep learning. That same year he and James McClelland published the two volume Parallel Distributed Processing, Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition, which brought connectionist ideas to a wide audience of psychologists, neuroscientists and computer scientists. He returned to Stanford as a professor in 1987, continuing his work in cognitive science until a neurodegenerative illness ended his research career in the late 1990s. He died in Chelsea, Michigan, on March 13, 2011, at the age of 68.

timeline.event: Completes a PhD in mathematical psychology at Stanford University and joins the faculty at the University of California, San Diego
timeline.impact: Begins a research career applying mathematical models to human cognition

timeline.event: Publishes Learning Representations by Back Propagating Errors with Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams in Nature
timeline.impact: Introduces an efficient technique for training multilayer neural networks, widely credited with reviving neural network research

timeline.event: Co-publishes the two volume Parallel Distributed Processing with James McClelland
timeline.impact: Establishes connectionism as a major framework in cognitive science

timeline.event: Awarded a MacArthur Fellowship and returns to Stanford University as a professor
timeline.impact: Recognized for his contributions to cognitive science research

timeline.event: Elected to the National Academy of Sciences
timeline.impact: Honored for his contributions to cognitive psychology and neural network theory

timeline.event: Stops teaching due to a neurodegenerative illness
timeline.impact: Ends an active research career that had reshaped cognitive science and neural network theory

timeline.event: The Rumelhart Prize is established in his honor

timeline.event: Dies in Chelsea, Michigan, on March 13 at age 68
timeline.impact: Closes a career whose backpropagation work underlies much of modern deep learning

quick_facts: Born in Wessington Springs, South Dakota, in 1942
Earned a PhD in mathematical psychology from Stanford University in 1967
Co-authored the 1986 Nature paper on backpropagation with Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams
Co-authored Parallel Distributed Processing, Explorations in the Microstructure of Cognition with James McClelland in 1986
Elected to the National Academy of Sciences and awarded a MacArthur Fellowship
The Rumelhart Prize, established in 2000, is awarded annually in his honor for contributions to the formal analysis of human cognition

achievements.title: Learning Representations by Back Propagating Errors, 1986
achievements.impact: Co-authored with Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, this Nature paper demonstrated an efficient method for training multilayer neural networks and became foundational to modern deep learning.

achievements.title: Parallel Distributed Processing, 1986
achievements.impact: Co-edited with James McClelland, this two volume work established connectionism as a major framework for modeling human cognition.

achievements.title: MacArthur Fellowship, 1987
achievements.impact: Recognized for contributions to cognitive science and the mathematical modeling of mental processes.

achievements.title: Election to the National Academy of Sciences, 1991
achievements.impact: Honored for foundational contributions to cognitive psychology and neural network theory.

achievements.title: Rumelhart Prize
achievements.impact: Established in 2000 by the Robert J Glushko and Pamela Samuelson Foundation, the annual prize honors contributions to the formal analysis of human cognition and carries his name in recognition of his influence on the field.
